MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">Par Pharmaceutical Companies, Inc. operates primarily through its wholly owned subsidiary, Par Pharmaceutical, Inc. (collectively referred to herein as &#147;the Company,&#148; &#147;we,&#148; &#147;our,&#148; or &#147;us&#148;), in two business segments. &nbsp;Our generic products division, Par Pharmaceutical (&#147;Par&#148;), develops (including through third party development arrangements and product acquisitions), manufactures and distributes generic pharmaceuticals in the United States. &nbsp;Our branded products division, Strativa Pharmaceuticals (&#147;Strativa&#148;), acquires (generally through third party development arrangements), manufactures and distributes branded pharmaceuticals in the United States. &nbsp;The products we market are principally in the solid oral dosage form (tablet, caplet and two-piece hard-shell capsule), although we also distribute several oral suspension products, nasal spray products, and products delivered by injection. &nbsp;&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">On November 17, 2011, we completed our acquisition of Anchen Incorporated and its subsidiary Anchen Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (collectively referred to as &#147;Anchen&#148;), a privately held generic pharmaceutical company. &nbsp;Anchen became part of Par as of the acquisition date (see Note 2, &#147;Anchen Acquisition&#148;). &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">We divested FineTech Laboratories, Ltd, effective December 31, 2005. &nbsp;We transferred FineTech to a former officer and director of ours for no consideration. &nbsp;The FineTech divestiture is being reported as a discontinued operation in all applicable periods presented (see Note 18 <font style=FONT-FAMILY:Symbol>-</font> &#147;Discontinued Operations &#150; Related Party Transaction&#148;). &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><b>Note 1 </b><font style=FONT-FAMILY:Symbol><b>-</font> Summary of Significant Accounting Policies:</b></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Principles of Consolidation:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of Par Pharmaceutical Companies, Inc. and its wholly owned subsidiaries. &nbsp;All intercompany transactions are eliminated in consolidation. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Basis of Financial Statement Presentation:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">Our accounting and reporting policies conform to the accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (U.S. GAAP). &nbsp;The Financial Accounting Standards Board (&#147;FASB&#148;) codified all the accounting standards and principles in the Accounting Standards Codification (&#147;ASC&#148;) as the single source of U.S. GAAP recognized by the FASB to be applied by nongovernmental entities in preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP. &nbsp;Rules and interpretive releases of the Securities and Exchange Commission (the &#147;SEC&#148;) under federal securities laws are also sources of authoritative U.S. GAAP for SEC registrants. &nbsp;&nbsp;All content within the ASC carries the same level of authority. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Use of Estimates:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">The consolidated financial statements include certain amounts that are based on management&#146;s best estimates and judgments. &nbsp;Estimates are used in determining such items as provisions for sales returns, rebates and incentives, chargebacks, and other sales allowances, depreciable/amortizable lives, asset impairments, excess inventory, valuation allowance on deferred taxes, purchase price allocations and amounts recorded for contingencies and accruals. &nbsp;Because of the uncertainties inherent in such estimates, actual results may differ from these estimates. &nbsp;Management periodically evaluates estimates used in the preparation of the consolidated financial statements for continued reasonableness. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Use of Forecasted Financial Information in Accounting Estimates:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">The use of forecasted financial information is inherent in many of our accounting estimates, including but not limited to, determining the estimated fair value of goodwill and intangible assets, matching intangible amortization to underlying benefits (e.g. sales and cash inflows), establishing and evaluating inventory reserves, and evaluating the need for valuation allowances for deferred tax assets. &nbsp;Such forecasted financial information is comprised of numerous assumptions regarding our future revenues, cash flows, and operational results. &nbsp;Management believes that its financial forecasts are reasonable and appropriate based upon current facts and circumstances. &nbsp;Because of the inherent nature of forecasts, however, actual results may differ from these forecasts. &nbsp;Management regularly reviews the information related to these forecasts and adjusts the carrying amounts of the applicable assets prospectively, if and when actual results differ from previous estimates. &nbsp;&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Cash and Cash Equivalents</i>:</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">We consider all highly liquid money market instruments with an original maturity of three months or less when purchased to be cash equivalents.&nbsp; These amounts are stated at cost, which approximates fair value.&nbsp; At December 31, 2011, cash equivalents were held in a number of money market funds and consisted of immediately available fund balances. &nbsp;We maintain our cash deposits and cash equivalents with well-known and stable financial institutions.&nbsp;&nbsp;At December 31, 2011, our cash and cash equivalents were invested primarily in AAA-rated money market funds, which hold high-grade corporate securities or invested in government and/or government agency securities. &nbsp;We have not experienced any losses on our deposits of cash and cash equivalents to date.</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px" align=center>F-7</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px"> <hr> <p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">Our primary source of liquidity is cash received from customers. &nbsp;In 2011, we collected $941 million with respect to net product sales as compared to $1,098 million in 2010 and $1,140 million in 2009. &nbsp;Our primary use of liquidity includes funding of corporate acquisitions, general operating expenses, business development and product acquisition activities, normal course payables due to distribution agreement partners and capital expenditures. &nbsp;In addition to these normal course activities, our significant cash outflows included the payment related to the Anchen Acquisition of $412,753 thousand on November 17, 2011 and payments related to the settlement of certain AWP litigation of $154,000 thousand during the third quarter of 2011<font style=COLOR:#ff0000>. &nbsp;</font>&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The ability to monetize our current product portfolio, our product pipeline, and future product acquisitions and generate sufficient operating cash flows that along with existing cash, cash equivalents and available for sale securities will allow us to meet our financial obligations over the foreseeable future. The timing of our future financial obligations and the introduction of products in the pipeline as well as future product acquisitions may require additional debt and/or equity financing; there can be no assurances that we will be able to obtain any such additional financing when needed or on acceptable or favorable terms. </p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Concentration of Credit Risk:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">Financial instruments that potentially subject us to credit risk consist of trade receivables. &nbsp;We market our products primarily to wholesalers, drug store chains, supermarket chains, mass merchandisers, distributors, mail order accounts and drug distributors. We believe the risk associated with this concentration is somewhat limited due to the number of customers and their geographic dispersion and our performance of certain credit evaluation procedures (see Note 5 <font style=FONT-FAMILY:Symbol>-</font> &#147;Accounts Receivable - Major Customers&#148;). </p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Investments in Debt and Marketable Equity Securities:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">We determine the appropriate classification of all debt and marketable equity securities as held-to-maturity, available-for-sale or trading at the time of purchase, and re-evaluate such classification as of each balance sheet date in accordance with FASB ASC 320. &nbsp;Investments in equity securities that have readily determinable fair values are classified and accounted for as available for sale. &nbsp;We assess whether temporary or other-than-temporary unrealized losses on our marketable securities have occurred due to declines in fair value or other market conditions based on the extent and duration of the decline, as well as other factors. &nbsp;Because we have determined that all of our debt and marketable equity securities are available for sale, unrealized gains and losses are reported as a component of accumulated other comprehensive gain (loss) in stockholders&#146; equity. &nbsp;Any other-than-temporary unrealized losses would be recorded in the consolidated statement of operations. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:11px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px" align=justify><i>&nbsp;Inventories:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">Inventories are stated at the lower of cost (first-in, first-out basis) or market value. &nbsp;We establish reserves for our inventory to reflect situations in which the cost of the inventory is not expected to be recovered. &nbsp;In evaluating whether inventory is stated at the lower of cost or market, management considers such factors as the amount of inventory on hand, estimated time required to sell such inventory, remaining shelf life, remaining contractual terms of any supply and distribution agreements including authorized generic agreements, and current expected market conditions, including level of competition. &nbsp;Such evaluations utilize <a name=OLE_LINK35><a name=OLE_LINK36>forecasted financial information. &nbsp;We record provisions for inventory to cost of goods sold. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Property, Plant and Equipment:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">Property, plant and equipment are carried at cost less accumulated depreciation. &nbsp;The costs of repairs and maintenance are expensed when incurred, while expenditures for refurbishments and improvements that significantly add to the productive capacity or extend the useful life of an asset are capitalized. </p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify>&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>&nbsp;Depreciation and Amortization:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">Property, plant and equipment are depreciated on a straight-line basis over their estimated useful lives. Leasehold improvements are amortized over the shorter of their estimated useful life or the term of the lease. &nbsp;The following is the estimated useful life for each applicable asset group:</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <table style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; FONT-SIZE:10pt" cellpadding=0 cellspacing=0> <tr height=0 style=FONT-SIZE:0px> <td width=270> <td width=138 /> </tr><tr> <td width=270 style=MARGIN-TOP:0px valign=top> <p style=MARGIN:0px>Buildings </p></td> <td width=138 style=MARGIN-TOP:0px valign=top> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=center>10 to 40 years</p></td></tr> <tr> <td width=270 style=MARGIN-TOP:0px valign=top> <p style=MARGIN:0px>Machinery and equipment</p></td> <td width=138 style=MARGIN-TOP:0px valign=top> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=center>3 to 15 years</p></td></tr> <tr> <td width=270 style=MARGIN-TOP:0px valign=top> <p style=MARGIN:0px>Office equipment, furniture and fixtures</p></td> <td width=138 style=MARGIN-TOP:0px valign=top> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=center>3 to 7 years</p></td></tr> <tr> <td width=270 style=MARGIN-TOP:0px valign=top> <p style=MARGIN:0px>Computer software and hardware</p></td> <td width=138 style=MARGIN-TOP:0px valign=top> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=center>3 to 7 years</p></td></tr></table> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Impairment of Long-lived Assets:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px">We evaluate long-lived assets, including intangible assets with definite lives, for impairment periodically or whenever events or other changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying value of an asset may no longer be recoverable. &nbsp;If such circumstances are determined to exist, projected undiscounted future cash flows to be generated by the long-lived asset or the appropriate grouping of assets, is compared to the carrying value to determine whether impairment exists at its lowest level of identifiable cash flows. If impairment is identified, a loss is recorded equal to the excess of the asset&#146;s net book value over its fair value, and the cost basis is adjusted. &nbsp;&nbsp;Our judgments related to the expected useful lives of long-lived assets and our ability to realize undiscounted cash flows in excess of the carrying amounts of such assets are affected by factors such as ongoing maintenance and improvements of the assets, changes in economic conditions, our ability to successfully launch products, and changes in operating performance. &nbsp;In addition, we regularly evaluate our other assets and may accelerate depreciation over the revised useful life if the asset has limited future value. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px" align=center>F-8</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px"> <hr> <p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Costs of Computer Software:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:36px">We capitalize certain costs associated with computer software developed or obtained for internal use in accordance with the provisions of FASB ASC 350-40. &nbsp;We capitalize those costs from the acquisition of external materials and services associated with developing or obtaining internal use computer software. &nbsp;We capitalize certain payroll costs for employees that are directly associated with internal use computer software projects once specific criteria of FASB ASC 350-40 are met. &nbsp;Those costs that are associated with preliminary stage activities, training, maintenance, and all other post-implementation stage activities are expensed as they are incurred. &nbsp;All costs capitalized in connection with internal use computer software projects are amortized on a straight-line basis over a useful life of three to seven years, beginning when the software is ready for its intended use. </p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Research and Development Agreements: </i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px">Research and development costs are expensed as incurred. &nbsp;These expenses include the costs of our internal product development efforts, acquired in-process research and development, as well as costs incurred in connection with our third party collaboration efforts. &nbsp;Milestone payments made under contract research and development arrangements or product licensing arrangements prior to regulatory approval of the associated product are expensed when the milestone is achieved. &nbsp;Once the product receives regulatory approval we record any subsequent milestone payments as intangible assets. &nbsp;We make the determination to capitalize or expense amounts related to the development of new products and technologies through agreements with third parties based on our ability to recover our cost in a reasonable period of time from the estimated future cash flows anticipated to be generated pursuant to each agreement. &nbsp;Market (including competition), regulatory and legal factors, among other things, may affect the realizability of the projected cash flows that an agreement was initially expected to generate. &nbsp;We regularly monitor these factors and subject all capitalized costs to periodic impairment testing. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Costs for Patent Litigation and Legal Proceedings:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px">Costs for patent litigation or other legal proceedings are expensed as incurred and included in selling, general and administrative expenses.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Goodwill and Intangible Assets:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px">We determine the estimated fair values of goodwill and intangible assets with definite and/or indefinite lives based on valuations performed at the time of their acquisition in accordance with FASB ASC 350. &nbsp;Such valuations utilize forecasted financial information. &nbsp;In addition, certain amounts paid to third parties related to the development of new products and technologies, as described above, are capitalized and included in intangible assets on the accompanying consolidated balance sheets. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">Goodwill is tested for impairment annually using a two-step process. The first step is to identify a potential impairment, and the second step measures the amount of the impairment loss, if any. &nbsp;Goodwill is impaired if the carrying amount of a reporting unit&#146;s goodwill exceeds its estimated fair value. We performed our annual goodwill impairment assessment as of December 31, 2011, noting no impairment.</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:3px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">Definite lived intangibles are amortized on an accelerated or straight-line basis over their estimated useful life. This determination is made based on the specific asset and the timing of recoverability from expected future cash flows. </p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px">We review the carrying value of our long-term assets for impairment whenever events and circumstances indicate that the carrying value of an asset may not be recoverable from the estimated future cash flows expected to result from its use and eventual disposition. &nbsp;In cases where undiscounted expected future cash flows are less than the carrying value, an impairment loss is recognized equal to an amount by which the carrying value exceeds the fair value of assets.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px">As discussed above with respect to determining an asset&#146;s fair value and useful life, because this process involves management making certain estimates and because these estimates form the basis of the determination of whether or not an impairment charge should be recorded, these estimates are considered to be critical accounting estimates. &nbsp;We will continue to assess the carrying value of our goodwill and intangible assets in accordance with applicable accounting guidance. </p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:37px" align=justify>&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>&nbsp;Income Taxes:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We account for income taxes in accordance with FASB ASC 740. &nbsp;Deferred taxes are provided using the asset and liability method, whereby deferred income taxes result from temporary differences between the reported amounts in the financial statements and the tax basis of assets and liabilities, as measured by presently enacted tax rates. &nbsp;We establish valuation allowances against deferred tax assets when it is more likely than not that the realization of those deferred tax assets will not occur. &nbsp;In establishing valuation allowances, management makes estimates such as projecting future taxable income. &nbsp;Such estimates utilize forecasted financial information. </p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px" align=center>F-9</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px"> <hr> <p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">FASB ASC 740-10 clarifies the accounting for uncertainty in income taxes recognized in an enterprise&#146;s financial statements and prescribes a recognition threshold and measurement attribute for financial statement recognition, measurement and disclosure of tax positions that a company has taken or expects to be taken in a tax return.&nbsp; Additionally, FASB ASC 740-10 provides guidance on de-recognition, classification, interest and penalties, accounting in interim periods and transition.&nbsp; See Note 16, &#147;Income Taxes&#148;. &nbsp;</p> <p style="FONT-SIZE:8pt; MARGIN:0px">&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Revenue Recognition and Accounts Receivable Reserves and Allowances:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We recognize revenues for product sales when title and risk of loss transfer to our customers, when reliable estimates of rebates, chargebacks, returns and other adjustments can be made, and collectability is reasonably assured. &nbsp;Included in our recognition of revenues are estimated provisions for sales allowances, the most significant of which include rebates, chargebacks, product returns, and other sales allowances, recorded as reductions to gross revenues, with corresponding adjustments to the accounts receivable reserves and allowances (see Note 5 &#150; &#147;Accounts Receivable&#148;). &nbsp;In addition, we record estimates for rebates paid under federal and state government Medicaid drug reimbursement programs as reductions to gross revenues, with corresponding adjustments to accrued liabilities. &nbsp;We have the experience and access to relevant information that we believe are necessary to reasonably estimate the amounts of such deductions from gross revenues. &nbsp;Some of the assumptions we use for certain of our estimates are based on information received from third parties, such as customers&#146; inventories at a particular point in time and market data, or other market factors beyond our control. &nbsp;The estimates that are most critical to our establishment of these reserves, and therefore would have the largest impact if these estimates were not accurate, are our estimates of non-contract sales volumes, average contract pricing, customer inventories, processing time lags, and return volumes. &nbsp;We regularly review the information related to these estimates and adjust our reserves accordingly, if and when actual experience differs from previous estimates. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Distribution Costs:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We record distribution costs related to shipping product to our customers, primarily through the use of common carriers or external distribution services, in selling, general and administrative expenses. &nbsp;Distribution costs for 2011 were approximately $2.5 million, $2.5 million for 2010 and $2.4 million for 2009.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Earnings / (Loss) Per Common Share Data:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">Earnings / (loss) per common share were computed by dividing net income (loss) by the weighted average number of common shares outstanding. &nbsp;Earnings / (loss) &nbsp;per common share assuming dilution were computed assuming that all potentially dilutive securities, including &#147;in-the-money&#148; stock options, were converted into common shares under the treasury stock method.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify>&nbsp;<i>Fair Value of Financial Instruments:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The carrying amounts of our cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable and accrued liabilities approximate fair values based upon the relatively short-term nature of these financial instruments. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Concentration of Suppliers of Distributed Products and Internally Manufactured Products:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We have entered into a number of license and distribution agreements pursuant to which we distribute generic pharmaceutical products and brand products developed and/or supplied to us by certain third parties. &nbsp;We have also entered into contract manufacturing agreements for third-parties to manufacture some of our own generic products for us. &nbsp;For the year ended December 31, 2011, approximately 58% of our total net product sales were generated from such contract-manufactured and/or licensed products. &nbsp;We cannot provide assurance that the efforts of our contractual partners will continue to be successful, that we will be able to renew such agreements, or that we will be able to enter into new agreements in the future. &nbsp;Any alteration to or termination of our current material license and distribution agreements, our failure to enter into new and similar agreements, or the interruption of the supply of our products under such agreements or under our contract manufacturing agreements, could have a material adverse effect on our business, condition (financial and other), prospects or results of operations. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We produce all of our internally manufactured products at a manufacturing facility in New York and a manufacturing facility in California. &nbsp;A significant disruption at those facilities, even on a short-term basis, could impair our ability to produce and ship products to the market on a timely basis, which could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial position and results of operations.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Segments:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">FASB ASC 280-10 codifies the standards for reporting of financial information about operating segments in annual financial statements. &nbsp;Management considers our business to be in two reportable business segments, generic and brand pharmaceuticals. &nbsp;Refer to Note 19 &#150; &#147;Segment Information&#148;.</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:8px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px"><i>Contingencies and Legal Fees:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We are subject to various patent litigations, product liability litigations, government investigations and other legal proceedings in the ordinary course of business. &nbsp;Legal fees and other expenses related to litigation are expensed as incurred and included in selling, general and administrative expenses. &nbsp;Contingent accruals are recorded when we determine that a loss is both probable and reasonably estimable. &nbsp;Due to the fact that legal proceedings and other contingencies are inherently unpredictable, our assessments involve significant judgment regarding future events.</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px" align=center>F-10</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px"> <hr> <p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Debt Issuance Costs:</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We capitalize direct costs incurred with obtaining debt financing, which are included in other assets on the consolidated balance sheet. &nbsp;Debt issuance costs are amortized to interest expense over the term of the underlying debt using the effective interest method. &nbsp;We recognized amortized debt issuance costs of $1,400 thousand in the year ended December 31, 2011 (including $579 thousand for the write-off of debt issuance costs related to our unsecured credit facility that was replaced by our Senior Credit Facilities on November, 17, 2011 &#150; refer to Note 12, &#147;Senior Credit Facilities&#148;), $304 thousand in the year ended December 31, 2010, and $492 thousand in the year ended December 31, 2009. &nbsp;</p><a name=jump_exp_1> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Recent Accounting Pronouncements: </i></p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The FASB has issued Accounting Standards Update (&#147;ASU&#148;) No. 2010-27, <i>Other Expenses (Topic 720): Fees Paid to the Federal Government by Pharmaceutical Manufacturers</i>. &nbsp;This ASU provides guidance on how pharmaceutical manufacturers should recognize and classify in their income statements fees mandated by the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (PPACA) and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act, both enacted in March 2010, referred to as the &#147;Acts.&#148; &nbsp;The Acts imposed an annual fee on the pharmaceutical manufacturing industry for each calendar year beginning on or after January 1, 2011. &nbsp;An entity&#146;s portion of the annual fee is payable no later than September 30 of the applicable calendar year and is not tax deductible. &nbsp;A portion of the annual fee will be allocated to individual entities on the basis of the amount of their brand prescription drug sales (including authorized generic product sales) for the preceding year as a percentage of the industry&#146;s brand prescription drug sales (including authorized generic product sales) for the same period. An entity&#146;s portion of the annual fee becomes payable to the U.S. Treasury once a pharmaceutical manufacturing entity has a gross receipt from branded prescription drug sales to any specified government program or in accordance with coverage under any government program for each calendar year on or after January 1, 2011. &nbsp;The amendments in this ASU specify that the liability for the fee should be estimated and recorded in full upon the first qualifying sale with a corresponding deferred cost that is amortized to expense using a straight-line method of allocation unless another method better allocates the fee over the calendar year that it is payable. &nbsp;The annual fee is classified as an operating expense in the income statement. &nbsp;The amendments in this ASU were effective for calendar years beginning after December 31, 2010, when the fee initially became effective. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The FASB has issued ASU 2010-29, <i>Business Combinations (Topic 805): Disclosure of Supplementary Pro Forma Information for Business Combinations.</i> The amendments in this ASU affect any public entity, as defined by Topic 805, <i>Business Combinations, </i>that enters into business combinations that are material on an individual or aggregate basis. &nbsp;The amendments in this ASU specify that if a public entity presents comparative financial statements, the entity should disclose revenue and earnings of the combined entity as though the business combination(s) that occurred during the current year had occurred as of the beginning of the comparable prior annual reporting period only. &nbsp;The amendments also expand the supplemental pro forma disclosures to include a description of the nature and amount of material, nonrecurring pro forma adjustments directly attributable to the business combination included in the reported pro forma revenue and earnings. &nbsp;The amendments are effective prospectively for business combinations for which the acquisition date is on or after the beginning of the first annual reporting period beginning on or after December 15, 2010. The requirements of this ASU have been applied to the disclosures related to our acquisition of Anchen and will be applicable to any future business acquisitions we complete. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The FASB has issued ASU 2011-05, <i>Comprehensive Income (Topic 220): Presentation of Comprehensive Income</i>. &nbsp;This amendment of the ASC allows an entity the option to present the total of comprehensive income, the components of net income, and the components of other comprehensive income either in a single continuous statement of comprehensive income or in two separate but consecutive statements. &nbsp;In both choices, an entity is required to present each component of net income along with total net income, each component of other comprehensive income along with a total for other comprehensive income, and a total amount for comprehensive income. &nbsp;This ASU eliminates the option to present the components of other comprehensive income as part of the statement of changes in stockholders&#146; equity. &nbsp;The amendments to the ASC in this ASU do not change the items that must be reported in other comprehensive income or when an item of other comprehensive income must be reclassified to net income. &nbsp;This ASU must be applied retrospectively. &nbsp;The amendments to the ASC in this ASU are effective for us for fiscal years and interim periods within those years, beginning after December 15, 2011. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The FASB has issued ASU 2011-08, <i>Intangibles&#151;Goodwill and Other (Topic 350): Testing Goodwill for Impairment</i>. &nbsp;This amendment of ASC will allow an entity to first assess qualitative factors to determine whether it is necessary to perform the two-step quantitative goodwill impairment test. &nbsp;Under this amendment, an entity would not be required to calculate the fair value of a reporting unit unless the entity determines, based on a qualitative assessment, that it is more likely than not that its fair value is less than its carrying amount. &nbsp;The amendment includes a number of examples of events and circumstances for an entity to consider in conducting the qualitative assessment. &nbsp;This amendment to the ASC is effective for annual and interim goodwill impairment tests performed for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2011. &nbsp;Early adoption is permitted, including for annual and interim goodwill impairment tests performed as of a date before September 15, 2011, if an entity&#146;s financial statements for the most recent annual or interim period have not yet been issued. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px" align=center>F-11</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px"> <hr> <p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><b>Note 2 &#150; Anchen Acquisition:</b></p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:4px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">On November 17, 2011, through Par Pharmaceutical, Inc., our wholly-owned subsidiary, we completed our acquisition of Anchen Incorporated and its subsidiary Anchen Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (collectively referred to as &#147;Anchen&#148;) for $412,753 thousand in aggregate consideration (the &#147;Anchen Acquisition&#148;), subject to post-closing adjustment. &nbsp;Pursuant to the Agreement and Plan of Merger, dated as of August 23, 2011, as amended (the &#147;Merger Agreement&#148;), among Par Pharmaceutical, Inc. and Admiral Acquisition Corp. (&#147;Merger Sub&#148;), a wholly owned subsidiary of Par Pharmaceutical, Inc., on the one hand, and Anchen and Chih-Ming Chen, Ph.D. (&#147;Dr. Chen&#148;), as securityholders&#146; representative, on the other hand, Merger Sub was merged with and into Anchen, with Anchen surviving as a wholly owned subsidiary of Par Pharmaceutical, Inc. (the &#147;Merger&#148;). &nbsp;In connection with the consummation of the Merger, Par Pharmaceutical, Inc., Anchen, Dr. Chen and Merger Sub entered into an Agreement and Amendment to Merger Agreement, dated November 17, 2011 (the &#147;Amendment&#148;), in which the parties agreed to modify certain pre-Merger covenants and the timing and manner of payment of certain severance and other benefit obligations. &nbsp;The Amendment also reflects the parties&#146; agreement as to the source and manner of payment of certain expenses in connection with paying agent services.</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:4px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">Anchen was a privately-held generic pharmaceutical company until our acquisition. &nbsp;Anchen broadens our industry expertise (e.g., R&amp;D and manufacturing capabilities) and product pipeline, with 29 ANDAs filed and four key commercialized products. &nbsp;The operating results of Anchen from November 17, 2011 to December 31, 2011 are included in the accompanying Consolidated Statements of Operations, reflecting total revenues of $12,932 thousand and a loss from continuing operations of $3,642 thousand. &nbsp;The Consolidated Balance Sheet as of December 31, 2011 reflects the Anchen Acquisition, including goodwill, which represents the Anchen workforce&#146;s expertise in R&amp;D and manufacturing. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:4px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The Anchen Acquisition has been accounted for as a business purchase combination using the acquisition method of accounting under the provisions of ASC No.&nbsp;805, &#147;Business Combinations,&#148; (&#147;ASC 805&#148;). &nbsp;The acquisition method of accounting uses the fair value concept defined in ASC 820, &#147;Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures.&#148; &nbsp;ASC 805 requires, among other things, that most assets acquired and liabilities assumed in a business purchase combination be recognized at their fair values as of the Anchen Acquisition date and that the fair value of acquired in-process research and development (&#147;IPR&amp;D&#148;) be recorded on the balance sheet regardless of the likelihood of success of the related product or technology as of the completion of the Anchen Acquisition. &nbsp;The process for estimating the fair values of IPR&amp;D, identifiable intangible assets and certain tangible assets requires the use of significant estimates and assumptions, including estimating future cash flows, developing appropriate discount rates, estimating the costs, timing and probability of success to complete in-process projects and projecting regulatory approvals. &nbsp;Under ASC 805, transaction costs are not included as a component of consideration transferred and were expensed as incurred. &nbsp;The Anchen Acquisition related transaction costs expensed for the year ended December 31, 2011 totaled $8,264 thousand and were included in operating expenses as selling, general and administrative on the Consolidated Statements of Operations. &nbsp;The Anchen Acquisition related transaction costs for the year ended December 31, 2011 were comprised of investment bank fees ($5,013 thousand), accounting fees ($1,628 thousand), legal fees ($1,348 thousand), and other fees ($275 thousand). &nbsp;The excess of the purchase price (consideration transferred) over the estimated amounts of identifiable assets and liabilities of Anchen as of the effective date of the acquisition was allocated to goodwill in accordance with ASC 805. &nbsp;The purchase price allocation is subject to completion of our analysis of the<a name=eolPage42> fair value of the assets and liabilities of Anchen as of the effective date of the Anchen Acquisition. &nbsp;Accordingly, the purchase price allocation below is preliminary and may be adjusted upon completion of the final valuation. These adjustments could be material. &nbsp;The final valuation is expected to be completed as soon as practicable but no later than one year from the consummation of the acquisition on November 17, 2011. &nbsp;The establishment of the fair value of the consideration for an acquisition, and the allocation to identifiable tangible and intangible assets and liabilities requires the extensive use of accounting estimates and management judgment. &nbsp;We believe the fair values assigned to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed are based on reasonable estimates and assumptions based on data currently available.</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:4px; LINE-HEIGHT:11pt"><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; LINE-HEIGHT:11pt"><br></p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:3px"><b>Note 4 &#150; Fair Value Measurements:</b></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">FASB ASC 820-10 Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures defines fair value as the price that would be received for an asset or paid to transfer a liability (an exit price) in the principal or most advantageous market for the asset or liability in an orderly transaction between market participants on the measurement date. &nbsp;FASB ASC 820 requires that assets and liabilities carried at fair value be classified and disclosed in one of the following three categories:</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="PADDING-LEFT:72px; MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:-48px">Level 1: Quoted market prices in active markets for identical assets and liabilities. &nbsp;Active market means a market in which transactions for assets or liabilities occur with &#147;sufficient frequency&#148; and volume to provide pricing information on an ongoing unadjusted basis. &nbsp;Cash equivalents include highly liquid investments with an original maturity of three months or less at acquisition. We have determined that our cash equivalents in their entirety are classified as Level 1 within the fair value hierarchy.</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; PADDING-LEFT:72px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:3px; TEXT-INDENT:-48px">Level 2: &nbsp;Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities; or other inputs that are observable or can be corroborated by observable market data for substantially the full term of the assets or liabilities. &nbsp;Our Level 2 assets primarily include debt securities, including corporate bonds with quoted prices that are traded less frequently than exchange-traded instruments. &nbsp;All of our Level 2 asset values are determined using a pricing model with inputs that are observable in the market or can be derived principally from or corroborated by observable market data. &nbsp;The pricing model information is provided by third party entities (e.g., banks or brokers). &nbsp;In some instances, these third party entities engage external pricing services to estimate the fair value of these securities. &nbsp;We have a general understanding of the methodologies employed by the pricing services in their pricing models. &nbsp;We corroborate the estimates of non-binding quotes from the third party entities&#146; pricing services to an independent source that provides quoted market prices from broker or dealer quotations. &nbsp;We investigate large differences, if any. &nbsp;Based on historical differences, we have not been required to adjust quotes provided by the third party entities&#146; pricing services used in estimating the fair value of these securities. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; PADDING-LEFT:24px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px">Level 3: Unobservable inputs that are not corroborated by market data.</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; PADDING-LEFT:24px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; PADDING-LEFT:24px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px" align=center>F-14</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; PADDING-LEFT:24px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px"> <hr> <p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:20px; PADDING-LEFT:36px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px; TEXT-INDENT:-2px">Unless specific in nature, the amount of provision or reversal of reserves related to prior periods for chargebacks is not determinable on a product or customer specific basis; however, based upon historical analysis and analysis of activity in subsequent periods, we have determined that our chargeback estimates remain reasonable.</p> <p style="CLEAR:left; MARGIN-TOP:0px; FLOAT:left; MARGIN-BOTTOM:-2px; WIDTH:36px">(2)</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; PADDING-LEFT:36px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px; TEXT-INDENT:-2px">Includes amounts due to indirect customers for which no underlying accounts receivable exists and is principally comprised of Medicaid rebates and rebates due under other U.S. Government pricing programs, such as TriCare, and the Department of Veterans Affairs. </p> <p style="CLEAR:left; MARGIN-TOP:0px; FLOAT:left; MARGIN-BOTTOM:-2px; WIDTH:36px">(3)</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; PADDING-LEFT:36px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px; TEXT-INDENT:-2px">During the first quarter of 2010, the Company settled a dispute with a major customer and as a result recorded an additional reserve of $1,300 thousand. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; PADDING-LEFT:36px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px; TEXT-INDENT:-2px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; PADDING-LEFT:36px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px; TEXT-INDENT:-2px" align=center>F-16</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; PADDING-LEFT:36px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px; TEXT-INDENT:-2px"> <hr> <p /> <p style="CLEAR:left; MARGIN-TOP:0px; FLOAT:left; MARGIN-BOTTOM:-2px; WIDTH:36px">(4)</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; PADDING-LEFT:36px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px; TEXT-INDENT:-2px">During the third quarter of 2010, the Company settled a customer dispute related to the January 2009 metoprolol price increase. As a result, the Company recorded an additional reserve of $1,100 thousand. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; FONT-SIZE:1pt; MARGIN-BOTTOM:-1pt" /> <p style="CLEAR:left; MARGIN-TOP:0px; FLOAT:left; MARGIN-BOTTOM:-2px; WIDTH:36px">(5)</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; PADDING-LEFT:36px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:6px; TEXT-INDENT:-2px">In December 2010, we reached a settlement related to the routine post award contract review of our contract with the Department of Veterans Affairs for the periods 2004 to 2007 with the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Veterans Affairs. &nbsp;We had previously accrued approximately $10,500 thousand ($6,400 thousand net of related partnership consideration) in accrued government liabilities and payables due to distribution agreement partners on our consolidated balance sheet related to this matter. &nbsp;We reduced this accrual to $7,300 thousand ($3,800 thousand net of related partnership consideration), based on the settlement. &nbsp;Accordingly, we recognized approximately $2,600 thousand of income in the fourth quarter of 2010 as a change in estimate. &nbsp;The 2009 change in accrued liabilities recorded for prior period sales is principally comprised of a $1,400 thousand credit from the Medicaid drug rebate program related to a positive settlement based upon the finalization of a negotiation in the third quarter of 2009 pertaining to prior years. &nbsp;With the exception of the foregoing factor, there were no other factors that were deemed to be material individually or in the aggregate. </p> <p style="CLEAR:left; MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The Company sells its products directly to wholesalers, retail drug store chains, drug distributors, mail order pharmacies and other direct purchasers as well as customers that purchase its products indirectly through the wholesalers, including independent pharmacies, non-warehousing retail drug store chains, managed health care providers and other indirect purchasers. &nbsp;The Company often negotiates product pricing directly with health care providers that purchase products through the Company&#146;s wholesale customers. In those instances, chargeback credits are issued to the wholesaler for the difference between the invoice price paid to the Company by our wholesale customer for a particular product and the negotiated contract price that the wholesaler&#146;s customer pays for that product. &nbsp;Approximately 60% of our net product sales were derived from the wholesale distribution channel for the year ended December 31, 2011 and 61% of our net product sales were derived from the wholesale distribution channel for the year ended December 31, 2010. &nbsp;The information that the Company considers when establishing its chargeback reserves includes contract and non-contract sales trends, average historical contract pricing, actual price changes, processing time lags and customer inventory information from its three largest wholesale customers. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s chargeback provision and related reserve vary with changes in product mix, changes in customer pricing and changes to estimated wholesaler inventory.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">Customer rebates and incentive programs are generally provided to customers as an incentive for the customers to continue carrying the Company&#146;s products or replace competing products in their distribution channels with our products. &nbsp;Rebate programs are based on a customer&#146;s dollar purchases made during an applicable monthly, quarterly or annual period. &nbsp;The Company also provides indirect rebates, which are rebates paid to indirect customers that have purchased the Company&#146;s products from a wholesaler under a contract with us. &nbsp;The incentive programs include stocking or trade show promotions where additional discounts may be given on a new product or certain existing products as an added incentive to stock the Company&#146;s products. &nbsp;We may, from time to time, also provide price and/or volume incentives on new products that have multiple competitors and/or on existing products that confront new competition in order to attempt to secure or maintain a certain market share. &nbsp;The information that the Company considers when establishing its rebate and incentive program reserves are rebate agreements with, and purchases by, each customer, tracking and analysis of promotional offers, projected annual sales for customers with annual incentive programs, actual rebates and incentive payments made, processing time lags, and for indirect rebates, the level of inventory in the distribution channel that will be subject to indirect rebates. &nbsp;We do not provide incentives designed to increase shipments to our customers that we believe would result in out-of-the-ordinary course of business inventory for them. &nbsp;The Company regularly reviews and monitors estimated or actual customer inventory information at its three largest wholesale customers for its key products to ascertain whether customer inventories are in excess of ordinary course of business levels.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">Pursuant to a drug rebate agreement with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, TriCare and similar supplemental agreements with various states, the Company provides a rebate on drugs dispensed under such government programs. &nbsp;The Company determines its estimate of the Medicaid rebate accrual primarily based on historical experience of claims submitted by the various states and any new information regarding changes in the Medicaid program that might impact the Company&#146;s provision for Medicaid rebates. &nbsp;In determining the appropriate accrual amount we consider historical payment rates; processing lag for outstanding claims and payments; levels of inventory in the distribution channel; and the impact of the healthcare reform acts. &nbsp;The Company reviews the accrual and assumptions on a quarterly basis against actual claims data to help ensure that the estimates made are reliable. &nbsp;On January 28, 2008, the Fiscal Year 2008 National Defense Authorization Act was enacted, which expands TriCare to include prescription drugs dispensed by TriCare retail network pharmacies. &nbsp;TriCare rebate accruals reflect this program expansion and are based on actual and estimated rebates on Department of Defense eligible sales. </p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The Company accepts returns of product according to the following criteria: (i) the product returns must be approved by authorized personnel with the lot number and expiration date accompanying any request and (ii) we generally will accept returns of products from any customer and will provide the customer with a credit memo for such returns if such products are returned between six months prior to, and 12 months following, such products&#146; expiration date. The Company records a provision for product returns based on historical experience, including actual rate of expired and damaged in-transit returns, average remaining shelf-lives of products sold, which generally range from 12 to 48 months, and estimated return dates. &nbsp;Additionally, we consider other factors when estimating the current period return provision, including levels of inventory in the distribution channel, significant market changes that may impact future expected returns, and actual product returns, and may record additional provisions for specific returns that we believe are not covered by the historical rates. </p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px" align=center>F-17</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px"> <hr> <p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The Company offers cash discounts to its customers, generally 2% of the sales price, as an incentive for paying within invoice terms, which generally range from 30 to 90 days. &nbsp;The Company accounts for cash discounts by reducing accounts receivable by the full amount of the discounts that we expect our customers to take. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">In addition to the significant gross-to-net sales adjustments described above, we periodically make other sales adjustments. &nbsp;The Company generally accounts for these other gross-to-net adjustments by establishing an accrual in the amount equal to its estimate of the adjustments attributable to the sale.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The Company may at its discretion provide price adjustments due to various competitive factors, through shelf-stock adjustments on customers&#146; existing inventory levels. &nbsp;There are circumstances under which we may not provide price adjustments to certain customers as a matter of business strategy, and consequently may lose future sales volume to competitors and risk a greater level of sales returns on products that remain in the customer&#146;s existing inventory. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">As detailed above, we have the experience and access to relevant information that we believe are necessary to reasonably estimate the amounts of such deductions from gross revenues, except as described below. &nbsp;Some of the assumptions we use for certain of our estimates are based on information received from third parties, such as wholesale customer inventories and market data, or other market factors beyond our control. &nbsp;The estimates that are most critical to the establishment of these reserves, and therefore, would have the largest impact if these estimates were not accurate, are estimates related to contract sales volumes, average contract pricing, customer inventories and return volumes. &nbsp;The Company regularly reviews the information related to these estimates and adjusts its reserves accordingly, if and when actual experience differs from previous estimates. &nbsp;With the exception of the product returns allowance, the ending balances of accounts receivable reserves and allowances generally are processed during a two-month to four-month period.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><i>Use of Estimates in Reserves</i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We believe that our reserves, allowances and accruals for items that are deducted from gross revenues are reasonable and appropriate based on current facts and circumstances. &nbsp;It is possible however, that other parties applying reasonable judgment to the same facts and circumstances could develop different allowance and accrual amounts for items that are deducted from gross revenues. Additionally, changes in actual experience or changes in other qualitative factors could cause our allowances and accruals to fluctuate, particularly with newly launched or acquired products. &nbsp;We review the rates and amounts in our allowance and accrual estimates on a quarterly basis. If future estimated rates and amounts are significantly greater than those reflected in our recorded reserves, the resulting adjustments to those reserves would decrease our reported net revenues; conversely, if actual product returns, rebates and chargebacks are significantly less than those reflected in our recorded reserves, the resulting adjustments to those reserves would increase our reported net revenues. &nbsp;We regularly review the information related to these estimates and adjust our reserves accordingly, if and when actual experience differs from previous estimates. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">In 2011, Par launched propafenone, amlodipine and benazepril HCl, and budesonide and some other lower volume generic products. &nbsp;In 2010, Par launched chlorpheniramine/hydrocodone, omeprazole sodium bicarbonate, and zafirlukast. &nbsp;In 2009, Par launched clonidine and some other lower volume generic products. &nbsp;Strativa acquired and relaunched Nascobal<sup>&#174; </sup>in the second quarter of 2009. &nbsp;As is customary and in the ordinary course of business, our revenue that has been recognized for these product launches included initial trade inventory stocking that we believed was commensurate with new product introductions. &nbsp;At the time of each product launch, we were able to make reasonable estimates of product returns, rebates, chargebacks and other sales reserves by using historical experience of similar product launches and significant existing demand for the products. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p><a name=OLE_LINK50><a name=OLE_LINK54> <p style="MARGIN:0px; &#147;Restructuring Costs.&#148; &nbsp;We will continue to recognize revenue and all associated cost of sales as Oravig<sup>&#174;</sup> and Zuplenz<sup>&#174;</sup> are prescribed to patients based on an analysis of third party market prescription data, third party wholesaler inventory data, order refill rates, and all substantive quantitative and qualitative data available to us. &nbsp;In July 2011, Strativa returned the U.S. commercialization rights of Zuplenz<sup>&#174;</sup> to its development partner, MonoSol, as part of the resizing of our branded products division. &nbsp;In September 2011, Strativa executed a termination agreement with BioAlliance returning all Oravig<sup>&#174;</sup> rights and obligations to BioAlliance. &nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify>&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify>&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=center>F-18</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify> <hr> <p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><br>&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><i>Major Customers &#150; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px"><i>Intangible Assets Acquired in Anchen Acquisition</i></p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">On November 17, 2011, Par completed the Anchen Acquisition. &nbsp;Refer to Note 2, &#147;Anchen Acquisition&#148; for details of the transaction. &nbsp;As part of the Anchen Acquisition, we acquired intangible assets related to IPR&amp;D, products derived from developed technology, and a covenant not to compete from a former Anchen securityholder and employee. </p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px" align=center>F-21</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px"> <hr> <p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The fair value of the developed technology and in-process research and development intangible assets were estimated using the discounted cash flow method of the income approach. &nbsp;Under this method, an intangible asset&#146;s fair value is equal to the present value of the after-tax cash flows (excess earnings) attributable solely to the intangible asset over its remaining useful life. &nbsp;To calculate fair value, we estimated the present value of cash flows discounted at rates commensurate with the inherent risks associated with each type of asset. &nbsp;We believe that the level and timing of cash flows appropriately reflect market participant assumptions. &nbsp;Some of the significant assumptions inherent in the development of the identifiable intangible asset valuations, from the perspective of a market participant, include the estimated net cash flows by year by project or product (including net revenues, costs of sales, research and development costs, selling and marketing costs and other charges), the appropriate discount rate to select in order to measure the risk inherent in each future cash flow stream, the assessment of each asset's life cycle, competitive trends impacting the asset and each cash flow stream and other factors. &nbsp;The major risks and uncertainties associated with the timely and successful completion of the IPR&amp;D projects include legal risk and regulatory risk. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:5px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The value of IPR&amp;D ($126,700 thousand) was capitalized and accounted for as an indefinite-lived intangible asset and will be subject to impairment testing until the completion or abandonment of each project. &nbsp;Upon successful completion and launch of each project, we will make a separate determination of useful life of the IPR&amp;D intangible. &nbsp;Amortization expense of the related intangible assets will commence when each product is launched. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:5px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The remaining net book value of the related intangible asset related to developed products ($83,550 thousand) will be amortized over a weighted average amortization period of approximately nine years.</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The fair value of the covenant not to compete was estimated using the discounted cash flow method of the income approach first assuming no additional competition from the parties to the covenant not to compete and then assuming competition from the parties to the covenant not to compete. &nbsp;The level of competition was adjusted by such factors as the timing of FDA approval and the likelihood of competition over the term of the covenant not to compete. &nbsp;The remaining net book value of the related intangible asset ($8,542 thousand) will be amortized over approximately three years. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; for further details related to our acquisition of Anchen.</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:5px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The Credit Agreement contains customary representations and warranties, as well as customary events of default, in certain cases subject to reasonable and customary periods to cure, including but not limited to: failure to make payments when due, breach of covenants, breach of representations and warranties, insolvency proceedings, certain judgments and attachments and any change of control. &nbsp;&nbsp;The Credit Agreement also contains various customary covenants that, in certain instances, restrict our ability to: (i) incur additional indebtedness; (ii) create liens on assets; (iii) engage in acquisitions of other companies, products or product lines or mergers or consolidations; (iv) engage in dispositions of assets; (v) make investments, loans, guarantees or advances in or to other companies; (vi) pay dividends and distributions or repurchase capital stock; (vii) enter into sale and leaseback transactions; (viii) engage in transactions with affiliates; and (ix) change the nature of our business. &nbsp;In addition, the Credit Agreement requires us to maintain the following financial covenants: (a) a maximum leverage ratio, and (b) a minimum fixed charge coverage ratio. &nbsp;While initially unsecured, we could be obligated to secure our obligations under the Credit Agreement should our leverage ratio exceed a predetermined threshold for two consecutive quarters. &nbsp;We were in compliance with all financial covenants as of December 31, 2011. &nbsp;All obligations under the Credit Agreement are guaranteed by our material domestic subsidiaries, including Par Pharmaceutical, Inc., Anchen Incorporated, and Anchen Pharmaceuticals, Inc. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=justify><br></p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><b>Note 14 </b><font style=FONT-FAMILY:Symbol><b>-</font> Share-Based Compensation:</b></p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We account for share-based compensation as required by FASB ASC 718-10 Compensation &#150; Stock Compensation, which requires companies to recognize compensation expense in the amount equal to the fair value of all share-based payments granted to employees. &nbsp;Under FASB ASC 718-10, we recognize share-based compensation ratably over the service period applicable to the award. &nbsp;FASB ASC 718-10 also requires that excess tax benefits be reflected as financing cash flows. &nbsp;&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We grant share-based awards under our various plans, which provide for the granting of non-qualified stock options, restricted stock and restricted stock units to members of our Board of Directors and to our employees. &nbsp;Stock options, restricted stock and restricted stock units generally vest ratably over four years or sooner and stock options have a maximum term of ten years.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">As of December 31, 2011, there were approximately 4.8 million shares of common stock available for future stock option grants. &nbsp;We issue new shares of common stock when stock option awards are exercised. &nbsp;Stock option awards outstanding under our current plans were granted at exercise prices that were equal to the market value of our common stock on the date of grant. &nbsp;At December 31, 2011, approximately 0.5 million shares remain available under such plans for restricted stock and restricted stock unit grants.</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">During 2010, we accelerated the vesting of 86 thousand stock options and 19 thousand non-vested restricted shares in connection with the termination of our former chief financial officer. &nbsp;The effect of this termination resulted in additional compensation expense of approximately $800 thousand. &nbsp;We also accelerated the vesting of approximately 4 thousand restricted stock units for a member of our Board of Directors who retired in 2010. &nbsp;We also cash settled approximately 23 thousand restricted stock units for the retired Board member. &nbsp;The effect of the cash settlement resulted in additional compensation expense of approximately $300 thousand.</p> <p TEXT-INDENT:48px">The Black-Scholes stock option pricing model was developed for use in estimating the fair value of traded options, which have no vesting restrictions and are fully transferable. &nbsp;We have three distinct populations of optionees; the Executive Officers Group, the Outside Directors Group, and the All Others Group. &nbsp;The expected life of options represents the period of time that the options are expected to be outstanding (that is, the period of time from the service inception date to the date of expected exercise or other expected settlement) and is based generally on historical trends. &nbsp;Through 2010, we had used the &#147;simplified method&#148; for &#147;plain vanilla&#148; options described in FASB ASC 718-10-S99 Compensation &#150; Stock Compensation &#150; SEC Materials. &nbsp;The &#147;simplified method&#148; calculation is the average of the vesting term plus the original contractual term divided by two. &nbsp;In 2011, we modified our expected life weighted average assumption based on an actuarial study derived from historical exercise data. &nbsp;The risk-free rate is based on the yield on the Federal Reserve treasury rate with a maturity date corresponding to the expected term of the option granted. &nbsp;The expected volatility assumption is based on the historical volatility of our common stock over a term equal to the expected term of the option granted. &nbsp;FASB ASC 718-10 also requires forfeitures to be estimated at the time of grant and revised, if necessary, in subsequent periods if actual forfeitures differ from those estimates. &nbsp;It is assumed that no dividends will be paid during the entire term of the options. &nbsp;All option valuation models require input of highly subjective assumptions. &nbsp;Because our employee stock options have characteristics significantly different from those of traded options, and because changes in subjective input assumptions can materially affect the fair value estimate, the actual value realized at the time the options are exercised may differ from the estimated values computed above.</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; Grants With Internal Performance Conditions</i></p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px; LINE-HEIGHT:10.8pt">In January 2012, we issued restricted stock units with performance conditions (&#147;performance units&#148;) to our Chief Operating Officer and our President. &nbsp;The vesting of these performance units is contingent upon the achievement of certain financial and operational goals related to the Anchen Acquisition and corporate entity performance with cliff vesting after three years if the performance conditions and continued employment condition are met. &nbsp;The Compensation Committee of the Board of Directors can make a discretionary adjustment to the performance unit awards in a range from 0% to 20% of additional shares at the end of the three year vesting period, as long as we have cumulative net income in 2012, 2013 and 2014. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px; LINE-HEIGHT:10.8pt">&nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px; LINE-HEIGHT:10.8pt" align=center>F-30</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px; LINE-HEIGHT:10.8pt"> <hr> <p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px; LINE-HEIGHT:10.8pt">Our Chief Operating Officer and our President each received approximately 25 thousand performance units in January 2012 and could be awarded up to an additional 5 thousand shares each at the discretion of the Compensation Committee of the Board of Directors based on the achievement of the specified financial and operational goals. &nbsp;The value of the performance units awarded was approximately $1.7 million at the grant date. &nbsp;The recognition of expense related to these performance units will be assessed each quarter based on the projected achievement of the financial and operational goals. &nbsp;The value of any shares awarded at the discretion of the Compensation Committee of the Board of Directors will be recognized after the three year vesting based on the market price of any discretionary shares awarded.</p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; LINE-HEIGHT:10.8pt"><br></p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:3px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px"><i>Restricted Stock Grants With Market Vesting Conditions</i></p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">In 2008, we issued restricted stock grants with market vesting conditions. &nbsp;The vesting of restricted stock grants issued to certain of our employees was contingent upon multiple market conditions that were factored into the fair value of the restricted stock at grant date with cliff vesting after three years if the market conditions had been met. &nbsp;Vesting was contingent upon applicable continued employment condition and the Total Stockholder Return (&#147;TSR&#148;) on our common stock relative to the Company&#146;s stock price at the beginning of the three-year vesting period as compared to the TSR of a defined peer group of approximately 12 companies, and the TSR of the Standard and Poor&#146;s 400 Mid Cap Index (&#147;S&amp;P 400&#148;) over the three-year measurement period. &nbsp;The measurement period ended on December 31, 2010. &nbsp;The Company achieved the maximum level of performance under the program because the Company&#146;s TSR was greater than the 75<sup>th</sup> percentile TSR of the peer group and the Company&#146;s TSR was greater than the median of the S&amp;P 400 during the three-year measurement period. &nbsp;Approximately 454 thousand shares of common stock were earned as of the vesting date, January 11, 2011. &nbsp;Approximately 65 thousand shares were issued in 2008 by operation of the provisions of employment contracts for three senior executives whose employment with us was terminated. &nbsp;Approximately 339 thousand shares of common stock were distributed in January 2011. &nbsp;Approximately 115 thousand shares were cash settled upon the discretion of the Compensation Committee of the Board of Directors for approximately $4.1 million (pre-tax) in January 2011. &nbsp;In all circumstances, restricted stock granted did not entitle the holder the right, or obligate the Company, to settle the restricted stock in cash. &nbsp;</p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:6px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">At the grant date, the effect of the market conditions on the restricted stock issued to certain employees was reflected in their fair value. &nbsp;The restricted stock grants with market conditions were valued using a Monte Carlo simulation. &nbsp;The Monte Carlo simulation estimated the fair value based on the expected term of the award, risk-free interest rate, expected dividends, and the expected volatility for the Company, our peer group, and the S&amp;P 400. &nbsp;The expected term was estimated based on the vesting period of the awards (3 years), the risk-free interest rate was based on the yield on the Federal Reserve treasury rate with a maturity matching the vesting period (2.6%). &nbsp;The expected dividends were assumed to be zero. &nbsp;Volatility was based on historical volatility over the expected term (40%). &nbsp;Restricted stock that included multiple market conditions had a grant date fair value per restricted share of $24.78.</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The following table style=MARGIN:0px>&nbsp;</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px align=center>F-31</p> <p style=MARGIN:0px> <hr> <p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; MARGIN-BOTTOM:3px"><i>Cash-settled Restricted Stock Unit Awards </i></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">We grant cash-settled restricted stock unit awards that vest ratably over four years to certain employees. &nbsp;The cash-settled restricted stock unit awards are classified as liability awards and are reported within accrued expenses and other current liabilities and other long-term liabilities on the consolidated balance sheet. &nbsp;Cash settled restricted stock units entitle such employees to receive a cash amount determined by the fair value of our common stock on the vesting date. &nbsp;The fair values of these awards are remeasured at each reporting period (marked to market) until the awards vest and are paid. &nbsp;Fair value fluctuations are recognized as cumulative adjustments to share-based compensation expense and the related liabilities. &nbsp;Cash-settled restricted stock unit awards are subject to forfeiture if employment terminates prior to vesting. &nbsp;Share-based compensation expense for cash-settled restricted stock unit awards are recognized ratably over the service period. &nbsp;Cash-settled restricted stock unit awards do not decrease shares available for future share-based compensation grants. </p> <p style=MARGIN:0px><br></p> <p style="MARGIN:0px; TEXT-INDENT:48px">The impact on our results of operations of recording share-based compensation from cash-settled restricted stock units for the years ended December 31, 2011 was as follows ($ amounts in thousands):</p> <table style="MARGIN-TOP:0px; FONT-SIZE:10pt" cellpadding=0 cellspacing=0> <tr height=0
